segments.text: Come in, come in. Before we begin, how would you like me to address you? Your notes say Mrs. Adeyemi-Clarke, which is quite a mouthful.
Oh, call me Bisi, everyone does, even the residents. Mrs. Adeyemi-Clarke is what the tax people call me.
Doctor, I've left the thermometer reading and the pulse oximeter on the desk for you, I'll be just outside if you need the swab kit.
Thank you, Priya. Right, Bisi, the receptionist said this was a quick check, you work at a care home and you've been feeling a bit flu-ish. Tell me from the start.
Well, it's probably nothing. I came in because the manager at the home practically frogmarched me out. She says anyone with a sniffle has to be signed off before they go near the residents.
That makes sense, they're a vulnerable group. What have you actually noticed?
A scratchy throat, mostly. It started two days ago, and it's mild, really. I woke up on Tuesday feeling like I'd swallowed a cheese grater but nothing dreadful.
Mild, two days. Have you been short of breath at all?
No, none, my breathing's fine. I did the stairs at the home twice this morning before she sent me off.
Good. Care work is physical, isn't it. Tell me about your day-to-day, I'm always curious.

Oh, it's a lot. I'm at the home six days out of seven, mornings mostly. Lifting, washing, feeding, chatting. Mr. Hollis in room nine tells me the same joke every single day, and I laugh every single day.
That sounds like the best part of the job. And at home, who do you live with?
My daughter and her two little ones, so I'm covered in germs from both ends, to be honest. The youngest brought something home from nursery last week, so I wonder if that's where it started.
Quite possibly. Do you smoke at all?
I used to. Gave up smoking about two years ago, after thirty years of cigarettes, and I still miss them on a bad day.
Well done, that's a big achievement. Any other health problems I should have on your record?
Migraines, but only a few a year now. And irritable bowel syndrome, which flares when the home is short-staffed. Nothing else, thank goodness.
All right. Let me take a look at your throat. Open wide and say ah.
Aaah. Is it very horrible in there?
Your throat is a little red at the back, with no white patches. That's quite mild.
Is that good? It felt a lot worse from the inside.
Now your numbers, which Priya got ready for me. Blood pressure is 118 over 74, and your pulse is 84.
Temperature is 37.9, so just slightly raised. Oxygen saturation is 98 percent, and your breathing rate is 16 a minute.
Right. So I do have a temperature.
The manager will be insufferable, you know.
It's only just up. What matters is what we do about work. Because of who you look after, I'd like to do a swab for flu and COVID, so we know what you are dealing with before you go back.
Does that mean the stick up the nose? I hate that.
A bit of the nose and a bit of the throat, I'm afraid. It takes ten seconds. It's unpleasant but quick.
Ten seconds, I can survive anything for ten seconds. Mr. Hollis would say that's what the wife told him on the wedding night.

Ha, I'll leave that one with you. Priya will do the swab in the next room. And in the meantime, stay off work until the result is back, and then until you've gone a couple of days without a temperature.
The manager will love that. The rota will be in tatters.
Their problem, not yours. Rest, drink plenty of fluids, and wash your hands well at home around the little ones.
Whenever you're ready, Bisi, this way, please.
Coming. Thank you, doctor, I do feel a bit sillier now than I did on the way over.
Not at all, you did the right thing. Take care of yourself for a change.
